To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please read and share: fake blue pills and what to do if someone goes down

I'm not going to talk about Saturday or anyone involved. That's not mine to talk about, and the families don't need more guessing. But I've just come in from nights and I can't sit on this, because the police warning further down this page is getting scrolled past and it really matters.

There are blue tablets going round south Manchester being sold as diazepam or "Xanax". They're fake. Some have been found to have nitazenes in them, which are synthetic opioids that can be far stronger than heroin. Nobody taking one has any way of knowing what's in it. Neither does the person selling it.

Signs someone's in trouble:
- really, really drowsy, can't be woken properly
- pinpoint pupils (the black bit of the eye goes tiny, like a pin head)
- slow or noisy breathing, snoring or gurgling
- blue or grey lips

If you see any of that, RING 999 STRAIGHT AWAY.

I'm a nurse, and this is the bit I most want people to hear. A really common thing that happens (generally, not about anyone in particular) is that mates panic. They don't want anyone getting in trouble, so they put the person to bed to "sleep it off" and ring for help hours later. By then the brain has gone without enough oxygen for too long. The snoring that sounds like someone's sleeping can be someone who's struggling to breathe. Do not put them to bed. Do not leave them on their own. Ring 999, stay with them, put them on their side if they're breathing, and do what the call handler tells you.

Please don't worry about getting in trouble. The police have said it themselves in their warning: "Our priority is preserving life." Ringing 999 is never the wrong call.

There's also naloxone. It's a nasal spray that reverses opioid overdoses, and it can buy someone time until the ambulance gets there. You can get it free from Brightpath drug & alcohol service on Stockport Road (next to the launderette). Anyone can ask, you don't have to give your name, and the training takes about 10 minutes. They're open Mon-Fri 10-4, and till 7 on Thursdays. I'd honestly like to see one in every house with a teenager in it.

Parents, please talk to your kids THIS week. Not after half term, not when you get round to it. This week. I had the chat with my lad last night over his tea. I got the eye rolls, the "Mum I KNOW", all of it, but he listened. He even asked me what pinpoint pupils meant. That's the whole point. It doesn't have to be a big sit-down lecture. Just tell them what the pills look like, what the signs are, and that if a mate goes down they ring 999 and they will not be in trouble with you for doing it. Say that last bit out loud, because they need to hear it from you.

And I'll say this gently, because I know people are angry and frightened. Slagging the kids off helps no one. Kids who are scared of getting a hiding, or of being judged by the whole estate, are the ones who don't ring for help. That's the whole problem. If we want them to pick up the phone, they have to know the adults round here care more about them being alive than about who did what.

Teenagers, if any of you are reading this: you don't know what's in those pills. If someone you're with goes floppy, won't wake up or their breathing sounds wrong, ring 999. Don't wait. Don't put them to bed. You won't be the one in trouble, you'll be the one who helped.

Please SHARE this, don't just like it. Share it to your own page, send it to the parents' WhatsApp groups and your family chats, and show it to your kids. A like doesn't get it in front of the one teenager who needs to see it.

Look after each other x
